name: Richard Vague
one_line: A Texas-born credit-card banker turned financial historian and Pennsylvania banking regulator who has spent two decades arguing, with mountains of data, that runaway private debt — not government deficits — is what wrecks economies.
bio: Richard Wade Vague was born in 1956 in Wichita Falls, Texas, and educated at the University of Texas; he began his career in Austin banking before co-founding and running two of the era's biggest consumer credit-card banks, First USA (sold to Bank One in 1997) and Juniper Financial (sold to Barclays in 2004), then the retail energy firm Energy Plus (sold to NRG in 2011). Newly wealthy and based in Philadelphia, he reinvented himself as a data-driven amateur economist and philanthropist: managing partner of Gabriel Investments, chair of the Governor's Woods Foundation, editor of the daily nonfiction-excerpt newsletter Delanceyplace.com, trustee and press chairman at the University of Pennsylvania, and a fixture in the Institute for New Economic Thinking's orbit, where he built country-by-country private-debt datasets. From 2020 to 2023 he served as Pennsylvania's Secretary of Banking and Securities under Democratic Governor Tom Wolf, and later chaired the board of PSERS, the state's largest public pension fund. His books — The Next Economic Disaster (2014), A Brief History of Doom (2019), An Illustrated Business History of the United States (2021), The Paradox of Debt (2023), and a 2026 biography of early American banker Thomas Willing — trace one obsession: the relationship between credit, crisis, and inequality.
known_for: A Brief History of Doom (2019), a comparative anatomy of ~200 years of financial crises built around private-debt buildups
The Next Economic Disaster (2014), which proposed quantitative early-warning thresholds for credit crises
The Paradox of Debt (2023), a balance-sheet view of the whole economy arguing debt simultaneously drives growth, asset inflation, and inequality
The claim that private debt (household + business), not public debt, is the reliable predictor of financial crises
Advocacy for debt restructuring and a modern 'debt jubilee' — write-downs of household debt paired with bank recapitalization
Assembling long-run cross-country private-debt-to-GDP data (via the Private Debt Project / INET) as a public resource
Delanceyplace.com, his widely read daily nonfiction excerpt email
Practitioner-turned-analyst credibility: he ran mass-market credit card lending before diagnosing its dangers
school: Heterodox, post-Keynesian-adjacent credit-cycle analysis — the Minsky–Fisher tradition of debt-driven instability, married to empirical financial history and flow-of-funds (sectoral balance sheet) accounting. Not academic economics; he writes as a practitioner-historian and is closely associated with the Institute for New Economic Thinking.
lineage: Builds directly on Irving Fisher's debt-deflation theory, Hyman Minsky's financial instability hypothesis, and Charles Kindleberger's crisis narratives, with the empirical scaffolding of Reinhart and Rogoff, Schularick and Taylor's 'credit booms gone bust' work, the BIS credit-gap literature, and Mian and Sufi's House of Debt. His sectoral-balances method echoes Wynne Godley. He sits alongside contemporaries like Steve Keen, Michael Hudson, and Adair Turner in the private-debt camp, and his data work and jubilee advocacy have in turn been picked up by that network, by INET, and by journalists and policymakers looking for early-warning indicators of credit stress.
stance: Financial crises are not random accidents, policy errors, or moral failures of borrowers; they are the predictable end-stage of rapid private lending growth. When private debt rises fast relative to GDP from an already-high level, lenders fund overcapacity, loan quality quietly rots, and banks fail — the same script from 1819 to 2008. Government debt gets blamed because it balloons afterward, but it is the consequence, not the cause. And because aggregate debt is never really repaid, only rolled and grown, it steadily transfers income to creditors and asset-owners, which is why high-debt economies deliver weak growth alongside soaring net worth at the top. The remedy is therefore not austerity but restraining credit growth in real time and, when the overhang is already crushing, writing debt down deliberately rather than waiting for a crash to do it.
blind_spots: Critics reasonably charge monocausality: nearly every episode in his histories resolves into the same private-debt mechanism, which risks explaining everything and therefore predicting little. His quantitative tripwires (roughly a high private-debt-to-GDP level plus a sharp multi-year surge) are rules of thumb fitted to a modest number of episodes, vulnerable to overfitting and to false positives — China has sat in his danger zone for years without the crisis his framework implies. Mainstream economists dispute his near-dismissal of public debt sustainability and think he sometimes slides from accounting identities (one sector's debt is another's asset) into causal claims. His jubilee proposals are thin on legal mechanics, moral hazard, and who bears the loss; his aggregate ratios can obscure who holds the debt and on what terms; and he underweights monetary policy, external imbalances, and regulatory structure. There is also an unavoidable irony his critics raise: he made his fortune mass-marketing exactly the kind of consumer credit he now warns about, and he writes outside peer review, so his work is influential in policy and journalism more than in academic literature.
politics: Discernibly center-left in party terms but not ideological in his economics. Wikipedia lists him as a Democrat, and he served as a gubernatorial appointee of Democratic Governor Tom Wolf as Pennsylvania's banking secretary and as a Wolf appointee to the PSERS pension board; his sympathies for household debt relief, student-loan write-downs, and his framing of inequality as a debt phenomenon read as progressive. But he is not a partisan writer: his diagnosis blames private lenders rather than any political faction, he is dismissive of deficit hysteria on both left and right, he has presented his work to business and free-market audiences including the Cato Institute, and his career and philanthropic circles are thoroughly establishment-business. Treat him as a Democratic-leaning financier-technocrat rather than a movement figure — he rarely litigates culture-war or electoral questions in print.
public_views: Watch private debt, not public debt: the ratio of household and business debt to GDP is the single best crisis warning sign available.
A rapid multi-year surge in private debt from an already-elevated base is the near-universal precondition for banking crises.
Runaway lending creates overcapacity — too many houses, too many factories, too many malls — and overcapacity is what ultimately makes the loans bad.
Debt in the aggregate is never paid down; it is refinanced and grows, which mechanically transfers income and wealth toward creditors and asset holders.
High debt loads are a structural drag on growth, which is why recoveries after credit busts are so anemic.

Deliberate debt restructuring — a modern jubilee, targeted at household debt like mortgages and student loans and paired with recapitalizing lenders — is preferable to a decade of grinding deleveraging.
Bailing out banks while leaving household balance sheets intact, as in 2008–09, treated the symptom and left the disease.
Wealth concentration and asset-price inflation are two sides of the same credit-expansion coin, not separate problems.
Government deficits often reflect private-sector distress rather than causing it, so austerity in a debt overhang is counterproductive.
Financial history is usable, not decorative: the patterns repeat closely enough that regulators could act on them if they chose to.
interview_notes: He presents as the opposite of a doom-monger despite his book titles: unhurried, plainspoken, avuncular, faintly Texan, and relentlessly empirical. Interviews and talks tend to be chart-led — he will reach for a debt-to-GDP series rather than a slogan — and he is careful to frame his conclusions as what the data show rather than as ideology, which makes him unusually welcome across podcasts, think tanks, and business audiences of different persuasions. Recurring moves: the long historical sweep (1819, 1857, 1873, 1929, Japan 1989, Asia 1997, 2008 as variations on one script), the insistence that the problem is lenders rather than feckless borrowers, mild exasperation that policymakers obsess over federal debt, and a genuine optimism that crises are preventable. He is candid and a little wry about his own past as a credit-card banker, and his omnivorous reading — the byproduct of running a daily nonfiction excerpt newsletter — surfaces as historical digressions and a fondness for anecdote.
personal: Born in Wichita Falls, Texas, and a University of Texas graduate; he came up through Austin banking rather than Ivy League economics, and the outsider's vantage shows in his willingness to ignore academic convention. Running First USA and Juniper put him at the center of the 1990s consumer-credit explosion, which is the formative experience behind his later work: he watched, from the inside, how lending growth and loan quality diverge. Now a Philadelphia philanthropist and civic fixture — Penn trustee, chair of the University of Pennsylvania Press, chair of FringeArts, board member of the Franklin Institute, Museum of the American Revolution, and PAFA — he also edits Delanceyplace.com, a daily excerpt from mostly historical nonfiction, which doubles as the engine of his own reading and the source of his historian's instincts.
key_topics: debt jubilee and household debt relief
